The Iowa-class. The largest and most powerful battleships ever built by any nation, representing the culmination of battleship design. Built primarily during World War II, four ships of the class—USS Iowa, USS New Jersey, USS Missouri, and USS Wisconsin—served as the capital ships of the American Navy. These vessels combined massive firepower, heavy armor, and unprecedented speed, embodying the height of twentieth-century naval technology before the carrier became the dominant warship. The Iowa-class displaced forty-five thousand tons fully loaded, making them the heaviest battleships in operation. Each carried nine sixteen-inch guns as primary armament capable of firing twenty-seven-hundred-pound shells over twenty miles—the most powerful naval artillery of their era. They featured a revolutionary hull design allowing speeds of thirty-three knots, or thirty-eight miles per hour, making them the fastest battleships of their era. This "fast battleship" design allowed them to operate with carrier task forces rather than as separate battle lines. The class entered service between nineteen forty-three and nineteen forty-four—USS Iowa, New Jersey, Missouri, and Wisconsin—arriving late enough to see limited combat service in the Pacific but carrying significant firepower in fleet operations and shore bombardment. USS Missouri is the most famous of the class, serving as the site of the formal Japanese surrender ceremony in September nineteen forty-five in Tokyo Bay. The ship became a symbol of American naval supremacy and remains a tourist attraction today. After World War II, the class was extensively modernized with upgraded missiles, fire-control systems, and sensors. They continued service through the Cold War as symbols of American naval might, with some remaining active into the nineteen nineties. USS Wisconsin and Missouri served in the nineteen ninety-one Persian Gulf War. The Iowa-class combined traditional big-gun firepower that battleship enthusiasts valued for psychological impact and survivability with modern radar, fire-control systems, guided missiles, and anti-aircraft armament, embodying the transition from gun-based to missile-based naval warfare. Their construction represented an enormous investment of resources during wartime—each cost over one hundred million dollars in nineteen forty dollars. This demonstrated American industrial capacity, naval ambition, and the belief that battleships would remain the dominant warship, though carrier warfare proved this assumption wrong.
